support_summary: D1: four author-defined cardiology (CRT) topics arranged in a 2x2 maturity/specificity matrix with standardized prompts (Methods), a small hand-picked set in one narrow subdomain; D2: complete prompts in Supplementary Table S2, tools accessed via free web interfaces Aug 2025-Jan 2026, ChatGPT-5 queried using the GPT-5 model; D4/D5/D6: references 'manually verified by the investigators' by DOI and title searches with no verification database named and no duplicate verification of bibliographic accuracy reported - the triple blinded expert rating (Fleiss kappa 0.72) covered relevance, not existence; D7: minor discrepancies classed locatable/corrected and only citations 'not traced to any identifiable source after DOI and title searches' classed hallucinated, counted apart (0 in main analysis; 10/59 in the clinical-studies subanalysis).

D1: 10 clinician questions sourced from North American Spine Society guidelines plus 10 author-written patient counterparts (Methods; Supplemental Digital Content 1) - a small guideline-based set; D2: both persona prompts printed verbatim and queries performed October 2025 on default web interfaces, but Microsoft Copilot carries no version (ChatGPT 5.0, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, OpenEvidence 2.7.12 are versioned); D3: internet search enabled for all, temperature 'not recorded', and a stated re-prompt rule when more than 5 citations were generated; D5: citations 'manually verified by the authors' with generation/verification roles not separated; D6: three independent medical student reviewers, 95.4% agreement, Cohen kappa 0.918, discordant scores resolved by consensus with the senior author; D4/D7: verification on PubMed and publisher websites across authors/title/year/journal/PMID/DOI, with Score 2 accurate / 1 misrepresented / 0 fabricated counted apart (Table 1).

D4: 'A fabricated reference was defined as a reference cited by ChatGPT but not indexed in PubMed' (Response Assessment) - fabrication is defined by a single database, so real references outside PubMed are counted fabricated by construction; D1: all 19 recommendations of the AAOS hip fracture CPG were queried (complete enumerated frame) from physician, patient and general perspectives; D2: ChatGPT Version 4o mini free public version, prompts submitted Oct-Nov 2024 in new private browsing windows, but full prompt wording is not printed in the main text; D5/D6: the same 4 medical student graders submitted the prompts and 'independently assessed' responses, with no per-reference duplicate grading or agreement statistic for citation grading; D7: fabrication and field-level inaccuracies (title, authors, journal, year, pages, volume, PMID) defined in Methods and counted apart (Table III).

D1: 14 author-written questions on a single topic (midshaft clavicle fractures), printed in full in Table 1 (4 patient-focused, 10 clinical); D2: ChatGPT-4o mini prompted on August 31, 2024 with the verbatim Table 1 questions; D3: each question submitted three times the same day in separate chat sessions with all 42 responses and 128 references analysed, but no generation settings are reported; D4: references 'verified through independent searches conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus' including titles, abstracts, keywords and authors; D5/D6: responses independently evaluated by two registrars (CK, RC) and two senior surgeons (MS, BS) - the author team itself - with no agreement statistic or settlement process reported for reference grading; D7: correct / incorrect (locatable with wrong title, authors, date or journal) / fabricated (could not be located at all) defined in Methods and counted apart (1 / 14 / 113).

D1: 8 author-written questions on a single topic (Achilles tendon rupture), printed in Table 1 - patient questions 1-4 anticipated from Google Trends searches, clinical questions 5-8 author-written; D2: ChatGPT 3.5 presented with the verbatim questions on February 6, 2024 (Methods; Limitations note the free version used in Australia); D3: each question entered twice with all 16 responses and 47 references analysed, but no generation settings are reported; D4: reference accuracy 'verified by conducting searches across MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus'; D5/D6: responses independently evaluated by two registrars (CK, RC) and two senior surgeons (MS, BS), the author team, with no agreement statistic for reference grading; D7: correct / incorrect (inaccurate title, authors, date or journal) / fabricated (could not be found) counted apart (16 / 19 / 12).

D5/D6: the paper never states who verified the 115 citations or whether verification was duplicated or blinded - queries were run by one author (LSM) and citations were 'documented' and title-searched, with no verifier named (Methods); D1: the 47 medications were aggregated from the FDA-approved list and the AAN 2012 guideline, with 5 pre-specified negative controls; D2: prompt printed verbatim ('is [medication] an effective medication for the prevention of migraine? Give 3 citations if they exist'), ChatGPT-3.5, new session with history cleared, queried April 14 and 16, 2023; D3/D4: single run per medication with no generation settings reported, and existence was settled by title searches on Google Scholar and PubMed only, so field-level accuracy beyond the title was not systematically checked; D7: real (33) / hallucinated (76) / real-paper-name with no real citation (6) counted apart.

D1: 20 cases author-developed from the most frequent presentations at one restorative dentistry clinic plus textbooks and exam banks, retained only if Lawshe content validity index >=0.62 from 10 experts; D2: exact versions and URLs for all five models (ChatGPT-5, DeepSeek V3.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Copilot, Gemini 3 Flash), all accessed December 25, 2025 on free-tier web interfaces, three-step prompt structure with step 2 verbatim but the follow-up reference request only paraphrased; D3: default settings (temperature not manually adjustable), web browsing enabled, history disabled, new session per question, each case queried once with no regeneration; D4: all references searched in PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus and Web of Science, fabricated only if retrievable from no database; D5/D6: reference assessments 'conducted independently by both study authors' (who also prepared and submitted the prompts) with consensus on disagreement but no agreement figure for references - the reported ICC covers the 42 specialists' Likert ratings; D7: four categories (accurate and relevant / partially accurate / misleading-irrelevant / fabricated) defined in Methods and counted apart per model (Table 3).

D1: a 40-question bank built from literature and clinical consultation experience, from which 10 high-priority questions were selected by an independent caregiver screening cohort (N=34, cohort A) - priority selection by design, not a random or complete frame; D5: reference authenticity was verified by 2 reviewers (XH and WH), both authors, and who generated the LLM responses is not stated, so generation/verification separation cannot be confirmed; all other domains low - the complete access protocol (URLs, model versions, browser environment, session management, configuration parameters, full Chinese/English prompt set) is in Multimedia Appendix 1, free-tier web interfaces in April 2025, verification followed a PubMed -> CrossRef DOI resolver -> Google Scholar -> CNKI hierarchy by 2 independent reviewers with Cohen kappa 0.702 pre-adjudication and canonical-source reverification, under a 5-category V/PV/F/G/NR scheme counted apart.

D2: the model is named only as GPT-4 (OpenAI) with no version string and no generation period stated, and the interface is not stated - the run cannot be placed in time (Methods); D4: 'Each reference was verified through direct links or a Google search' - 3,250 references checked on a single general web search with no bibliographic database and no second source before 383 were called hallucinated; D5/D6: who applied the Reference Evaluation for AI tool, and whether reference verification was duplicated or blinded, is never stated (the 3 plastic surgeons rated content with NLAT-AI, not references); D1: 354 questions manually collected by the authors from the Hot pages of r/Keloids, r/SCAR and r/PlasticSurgery as of April 6, 2025 plus questions from 3 medical websites; D3: questions input individually in independent sessions with no appended instructions, settings unreported; D7: references are split only into real (2,867) vs hallucinated (383), with no rule or count for real references carrying wrong fields.

D3/D5/D6: no generation settings are reported anywhere, and the paper never states who verified the references or whether that verification was duplicated or blinded - the seven ophthalmologists independently rated anonymised reviews for quality/accuracy/bias/relevance (ICC reported), but the authenticity check is described only as 'all cited references underwent a rigorous authenticity check' with no actor (Methods); D1: nine SMILE topics chosen and classified by 3 experts (consensus of at least 2) into researched / controversial / open, three per group, listed in Table 1; D2: the standardised prompt is printed verbatim ('Write a 1,500-word literature review on the topic...'), free/basic versions of GPT-4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok-3 and DeepSeek R1, but no generation date or interface is stated; D4: references 'manually retrieved and verified through academic databases such as PubMed and Google Scholar', the source set left open by 'such as'; D7: True and relevant / True but not relevant / Fictitious counted apart, but no category or rule covers a real publication cited with wrong fields.

D7: references 'located within these databases and pertinent to the query content were classified as verified, those unavailable or irrelevant were classified as unverified' (Methods), and Table 5 relabels the unverified count as Fabricated - real but irrelevant references are folded into the fabricated count with no split printed; D2/D5/D6: models are named (Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-0528, ChatGPT o3-pro, Gemini 2.5 pro, Claude 4.0) and all 110 questions were entered on June 5, 2025 with session resets, but the exam questions are not reproduced and who searched the references, or whether that search was duplicated, is not stated - the two other researchers evaluated answer correctness against the official key; D1: all OMFS multiple-choice questions from the CNMLE dentistry category 2013-2024 (complete frame, n=110); D3: generation parameters fixed for open-source models (temperature 0.7, top_k 40, top_p 0.9), proprietary models at defaults; D4: Chinese references checked in CNKI and Wanfang, English references in PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar.

D2: 'Terminology was not established in advance, and participants reported chatbot versions inconsistently' - of 5 Claude users 1 reported paid, 2 reported 3.5 and 2 free/unspecified, and Gemini, OpenEvidence and Perplexity users all indicated free or unspecified versions, so each tool arm pools unrecorded versions (Methods); sessions ran Aug-Sept 2024 and both prompts are printed verbatim; D1: only two author-developed prompts (Teach-Back at discharge; neutropenic diet and sepsis) each with three standardised 'additional' follow-ups; D3: prompts repeated three times per tool by 4-7 librarians per tool with OpenEvidence limited to two follow-ups at the free level, settings otherwise unreported; D5/D6: librarians both submitted prompts and verified citations, duplicate checking with a third-researcher tie-breaker is stated only for relevance, not for the hallucination call, and no agreement figure is given; D4: each citation searched in PubMed, the journal if listed, and via web search before being called a hallucination; D7: 'we counted as real any citation for which we found a close/complete match', so field-level partial errors are folded into the real count with no partial count printed.

D3: physicians themselves iterated each LLM interactively - 'the number of iterations required by the physician to either achieve LLM generation of a satisfactory response, or discontinue attempting to do so, was documented' - so the verified reports are satisfaction-selected final outputs, iteration counts varied by user and model, 23 LLM reports contained no references despite several prompts, and 4 Gemini reports were lost to a technical malfunction; D1: 27 queries self-selected by purposively sampled physicians from their own complex cases, 20 retained after pre-specified exclusions; D2: GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 and Claude Sonnet 3.5 accessed via standard web interfaces, but no generation dates are stated and the individual clinical queries are not printed; D4-D8 low: existence verified through PubMed and Google Scholar (direct URL for websites) with full-text faithfulness checks, report quality evaluated post-hoc by an independent researcher blinded to report source and to satisfaction, and hallucinated / unfaithful / irrelevant citations counted apart in sequence.

D6: the citation audit is described only as 'an independent post hoc audit of all AI-generated references' - whether it was duplicated or blinded and how disagreements were settled is not stated, and the reported ICCs cover the blinded panel's Likert ratings, not the audit; D5: the audit's performer is not named; D1: two hand-picked topics (chronic rhinosinusitis; infantile subglottic hemangioma, one common and one rare); D2: section-by-section prompt templates in Table 1, standard conversational interfaces with browsing/deep-research features explicitly not enabled, generation in triplicate across April 2025, but models are named only as GPT-4.0 and Gemini 2.0 with no exact release strings; D7: the four audit categories (fully accurate / minor metadata discrepancy / duplicate / fabricated or corrupted) were set in a post hoc audit rather than in advance, though counts are given per model (GPT-4.0 89.6% fully accurate, 0% fabricated; Gemini 2.0 71.7%, 23.9%); D3/D4/D8 low: fresh sessions, identical prompts, the first chronologically generated iteration pre-selected for evaluation, verification against PubMed and journal websites by exact title and author matching, and all topics, styles and models reported.

D4: no verification source or procedure for references is stated anywhere - Gemini's citations are described as '32 PubMed articles... with links provided' and ChatGPT's nonexistent studies were identified narratively, in one case only after a follow-up link request drew an apology, so the fabrication calls rest on no named, systematic check (Methods; Results; Tables III-IV); D1: queries were patient-style rephrasings of the 12 strong- or moderate-strength AAOS glenohumeral arthritis CPG recommendations, with limited-strength and consensus recommendations excluded for a stated reason; D3: each query submitted once on a single day, but all queries went through one continuing anonymous session (authors' limitation: later responses may have been shaped by earlier ones) and links were elicited by follow-up requests; D5/D6: two authors (S.M.O., S.B.P.) independently classified responses with a third tie-breaker and Cohen kappa 0.84, but that duplication covers CPG concordance, not the reference calls, which are unattributed; D7: headline counts fold the two failure modes together ('nonexistent or inappropriately cited': ChatGPT 4/6, Gemini 5/32), separated only in narrative examples; D2 low: models GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Pro, submitted April 30, 2025, queries printed in Table I.

D8/D6/D7: references were collected and checked for only one of the four models - after rating, 'the model with the highest overall ratings was identified' and that model alone 'was then asked to provide references', so the citation outcome covers a single arm selected on results; verification was by a single IT engineer ('an IT engineer was responsible for verifying the accuracy of the references') with no duplicate or blinded check; and 'the verification focused solely on the existence of these sources', with no partial-match rule, yet all 101 GPT-4 references are reported as '100% accurate'; D4: the source the engineer checked existence against is never named; D1: 21 nephrology questions curated by experienced nephrologists (7 dialysis, 7 kidney examination, 7 general) plus 3 biopsy reports, questions listed; D2: GPT-4, Gemini 1.0 Ultra and PaLM 2 (via Bard) run Dec 8-12, 2023 and GPT-4o Oct 21-23, 2024 through official GUIs - arms run ten months apart - with the reference-request prompt not printed; D5: IT engineers both queried the models and verified the references.

D7: no rule for partial or false references is stated and no fabricated count is printed for either model - false material was simply removed ('by searching the reference materials... and eliminating false information, we derived the authentic reference materials'), and the only error count given is 4 invalid links for DeepSeek-R1 with no ChatGPT counterpart; D4/D6: references were 'manually searched' with no database or source named, and whether that search was duplicated or blinded is never stated (the two experts' blinded mDISCERN scoring covered answer accuracy, not references); D1: 45 questions gathered from patient surveys, 15 nurses and network searches, coded by two researchers and reduced to the '15 most pressing'; D2: a unified prompt is printed and interfaces are detailed (DeepSeek-R1 via official web platform in Chrome 126; ChatGPT-4.0 via the OpenAI API in Python 3.9.7), but no generation date is stated and ChatGPT is versioned only as 4.0; D3: temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95 and 2,048-token cap are reported, but the arms ran through different interfaces (web vs API) and the text also describes both as run at defaults with browsing plugins enabled; D5: the team that prompted the models also searched their sources.

D1: the ten neuroradiology tasks (5 essays, 5 evidence-based Q&A) were drawn from a topic pool initially generated by ChatGPT itself, with 'final topic selection and refinement performed independently by the authors'; D5: the two blinded raters (S.E., J.N.) also developed the evaluation framework a priori and selected the topics, though ratings were independent, outputs de-identified and the blinding key held by a non-rating co-author; all other domains low - all prompting on February 18, 2025 via public web interfaces (DeepSeek-R1 version R1 released January 2025; ChatGPT-o1 version o1 released December 2024), complete prompts in Supplementary Texts 1-2, parameters not user-configurable and left at provider defaults, identical phrasing in fresh sessions with cache cleared, references classified against PubMed and Google Scholar as gold standard plus DOI lookup as (a) fully verifiable, (b) partially correct, (c) unverifiable, or (d) fully fabricated (DOI resolving to a different publication), with counts apart per model and ICC/Cohen kappa reported.

D7: grades A-F are defined only 'if the title existed' and 'No grade was given for a fake title or no answer' (Quality Assessment of Answers; Table 1) - fabricated references fall outside the grading system entirely and no fabricated count is printed anywhere, so the 1,287 ChatGPT studies identified cannot be reconciled with the 403 graded (7 A, 18 B, 167 C, 211 F); partial-field mismatches among real titles are, by contrast, graded finely and counted apart (B/C/F); D5/D6: who graded the answers, and whether grading was duplicated or blinded, is never stated; D1: a single topic (Peyronie disease RCTs) taken from the benchmark systematic review by Lee et al, with question prompts built from its search formula in graduated specificity and the initial 'find' phrasing abandoned after ChatGPT returned no studies - the change is reported in the text; D2: ChatGPT GPT-3.5 and Bing AI (Prometheus/GPT-4 with web search), prompt format in Textbox 1, but no generation date is stated; D4: answers were checked by manually searching the named target databases (PubMed, Google Scholar, Cochrane Library, ClinicalTrials.gov) one by one under a printed title -> author/journal/year matching hierarchy; D8: the PubMed Research plug-in arm is reported only in the Discussion, without counts.
